query: Consider a TaVCrW refractory high-entropy alloy. The objective is to calculate its melting temperature and related thermodynamic properties using Density Functional Theory (DFT). The standard approach (TOR-TILD) relies on expensive thermodynamic integration. We hypothesize that substituting the reference potential (EAM) with a Machine Learning Interatomic Potential (MTP) and replacing thermodynamic integration with free energy perturbation (FEP) can achieve significant speedups while maintaining sub-meV accuracy, provided the MTP accurately reproduces the ab initio phase-space distribution even for complex liquids. Prior work suggests that electronic excitations (specifically the gap in the Density of States at the Fermi level) can shift the melting point by tens of Kelvin, and that Short-Range Order (SRO) in the solid phase can introduce a stabilization energy of ~2-3 meV/atom. However, there are limitations: (1) The empirical 'underbinding/overbinding' rules for GGA-PBE/LDA functionals do not hold for V and Cr at 0K, potentially propagating errors; (2) High-temperature magnetic fluctuations are typically neglected but may be relevant. The computational cost must be reduced by >80% compared to the baseline TOR-TILD method. Propose the specific structural mediator (the MTP's ability to reproduce phase-space distributions) that enables the substitution of TI with FEP. What is the boundary condition regarding the supercell size and temperature range (2000-2400 K) needed to validate the SRO contribution? Design a falsification experiment comparing the new method against the original TOR-TILD on a benchmark system (e.g., a simpler alloy) to ensure the free energy difference does not exceed 0.5 meV/atom.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting the EAM reference potential with a Machine Learning Interatomic Potential (MTP) trained on TaVCrW ab initio data, and replacing thermodynamic integration (TI) with free energy perturbation (FEP), will reduce the computational cost of calculating the melting temperature of TaVCrW by >80% while maintaining a free energy difference within 0.5 meV/atom of the baseline TOR-TILD method, provided the MTP accurately captures the Short-Range Order (SRO) stabilization energy of ~2-3 meV/atom in the solid phase and the electronic gap effects at the Fermi level.
generation.material_initial_state: TaVCrW refractory high-entropy alloy in a disordered body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution phase at 0 K, exhibiting potential underbinding/overbinding errors in GGA-PBE/LDA functionals for V and Cr, and possessing Short-Range Order (SRO) contributions of ~2-3 meV/atom.
generation.intervention: Replace the Embedded Atom Method (EAM) reference potential with a Moment Tensor Potential (MTP) trained on Density Functional Theory (DFT) data for TaVCrW, and replace the Thermodynamic Integration (TI) method with Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) for calculating the solid-liquid free energy difference.
generation.conditions: Temperature range of 2000-2400 K to capture the melting transition and SRO effects; Supercell size must be sufficient to capture the correlation length of SRO (estimated >100 atoms based on clustering behavior in similar HEAs) to validate the SRO contribution; Electronic excitations and magnetic fluctuations must be accounted for in the DFT training set or via post-processing corrections.
generation.structural_mediator: The MTP's ability to reproduce the ab initio phase-space distribution, specifically capturing the local atomic environments and Short-Range Order (SRO) configurations that contribute ~2-3 meV/atom of stabilization energy, which is critical for the FEP method to converge accurately without the extensive sampling required by TI.
generation.mechanism: The MTP provides a computationally efficient surrogate for the DFT energy landscape, allowing for the generation of the large number of configurations required for FEP sampling. By accurately reproducing the SRO and electronic gap effects (which shift melting points by tens of Kelvin), the MTP ensures the free energy perturbation estimates remain within the sub-meV accuracy threshold, bypassing the expensive thermodynamic integration path required by the TOR-TILD method.
generation.predicted_outcome: The calculated melting temperature of TaVCrW will be within 10 K of the baseline TOR-TILD result, with a free energy difference of <0.5 meV/atom, and the total computational time will be reduced by >80%.
generation.baseline: The standard TOR-TILD method using EAM potentials and thermodynamic integration, which is computationally expensive and relies on empirical rules that may fail for V and Cr at 0 K.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds only if the supercell size is large enough to capture the SRO correlation length (preventing finite-size errors in the ~2-3 meV/atom stabilization energy) and if the temperature range (2000-2400 K) is sufficient to sample the liquid phase and the solid-liquid coexistence region without significant magnetic fluctuation artifacts (which are currently neglected but may be relevant).
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the validity of the 'underbinding/overbinding' rules for V and Cr at 0 K in the DFT training data, which could propagate errors into the MTP. Additionally, the neglect of high-temperature magnetic fluctuations in the current DFT setup may introduce systematic errors in the free energy calculation, potentially exceeding the 0.5 meV/atom threshold if not corrected.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a benchmark calculation on a simpler refractory HEA system (e.g., NbMoTaW) using both the original TOR-TILD method (EAM + TI) and the proposed MTP+FEP method. Ensure the MTP is trained on high-fidelity DFT data for this system. Run simulations at the melting point and 200 K below/above to calculate the solid-liquid free energy difference.
measurements: Free energy difference (ΔF) between solid and liquid phases calculated by both methods.
Computational wall-clock time for each method.
Convergence of SRO parameters in the solid phase as a function of supercell size.
Melting temperature (Tm) derived from the intersection of free energy curves.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the absolute difference in the calculated free energy difference (ΔF_MTP+FEP - ΔF_TOR-TILD) exceeds 0.5 meV/atom, or if the computational time reduction is less than 80%, or if the predicted melting temperature deviates by more than 20 K from the baseline method without a clear physical justification (e.g., known magnetic effects).

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. The response of atoms to cluster or order in alloys offers deep insights to the microstructural behavior. This trend is particularly important for multi-component alloys, because the ordering can drive the system to various microstructural states, such as crystalline or intermetallic solids, from the disordered FCC ( A1 ), BCC ( A2 ), or HCP ( A3 ) conditions. In Al x CrCoFeNi, the Al content can influence the final structural configuration [6] [23] [24] [25] [26] [27] due to the larger atom size, compared to other constituents, which considerably changes the lattice ordering. When the mole fraction of Al <0.3, a single-phase A1 is observed, and a single-phase A2 is found for Al >1.17, while a two-phase ( A1 + A2 ) for 0.3 ≤ Al ≤1.17 is reported [24] [26] . Using the methods and approximations for accurate estimates of the formation enthalpy and relative energy of A1 and A2 phases [28] , the first-principles KKR-CPA results in Fig. 2 for Al of 0 < x < 2 mole fractions predict a similar global stability found in the experiment, i.e., A1 for x < 0.5, A1 + A2 for 0.5 ≤ Al ≤1.25, and A2 for Al > 1.25. The LSF methodology proposed by Dong et al . [29] , [30] was adopted to describe the finite-temperature magnetic state of each alloy species in PM CoCrFeMnNi HEA. The root-mean-square magnetic moment m I ( w , T ) [30] , which is formulated as m I = ∫ μ 2 ⋅ x ( μ ) d μ with x ( μ ) being the spin-density distribution of longitudinal magnetic component μ , was used to represent the LSF energetics at thermal excitations in both the fcc and hcp phases. For the sake of computational feasibility of determining { m I }, we used the ‘fluctuating medium approximation’ and the ‘one shot from static equilibrium approach’ [29] . The present LSF methodology has been applied to PM bcc and fcc Fe and Fe-Cr-Ni alloy, and the predicted finite-temperature properties such as single-crystal elastic constants [29] , [30] , lattice expansion [34] and intrinsic energy barriers [39] confirm the accurate description of the magnetic state at elevated temperatures.

Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] .
